activities.intendedInsight: The macrostructure should express the thesis argument, not only the sequence of research activities.
activities.rationale: Paltridge and Starfield (2020) recommend planning chapters around the overall argument and the examiner's reading of the whole thesis.

difficulties.pattern: A thesis is just a very long dissertation with the same chapters.
difficulties.revealedBy: Plans that copy a master's dissertation structure regardless of whether the research has several studies or is theory-led.
difficulties.response: Show alternative structures from the department and ask the learner to justify their choice by the shape of the research.

difficulties.pattern: In a thesis by publication, I just staple my papers together.
difficulties.revealedBy: Missing or minimal integrative chapters and repeated literature reviews across papers with no linking text.
difficulties.response: Discuss examiners' expectations of coherence and explain the institution's rules on framing chapters, co-authorship statements and overlap.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe their thesis structure and explain why it suits their research.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names a recognised structure, explains how it fits the design and argument, and shows awareness of regulations.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Has a reasonable plan but cannot justify it beyond 'this is the usual structure'.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Has no plan or applies an unsuitable structure without awareness of alternatives.

guidance.contextNotes: At PGT, the dissertation structure is usually prescribed by the programme, so the focus is on understanding it. At PGR, learners may choose among structures, and publication-based theses are increasingly common in some countries and fields, with institution-specific rules.

guidance.summary: In long texts, metatext operates above the paragraph: Bunton (1999) describes higher-level metatext in PhD theses that refers to chapters and to the thesis as a whole, and Hyland (2005) places frame markers, endophoric markers and code glosses within the interactive resources writers use to guide readers. Paltridge and Starfield (2020) discuss chapter introductions and conclusions as structural signposts. Teach metatext as reader guidance that should be accurate, proportionate and revised as the thesis changes.

activities.title: Skeleton read-through
learnerActions: Extract all chapter introductions and conclusions from a model thesis
Read them in sequence and summarise the thesis argument
Repeat the exercise with your own draft
Identify where the argument breaks down and revise the metatext
activities.intendedInsight: Chapter openings and closings carry the thesis argument for readers who navigate rather than read straight through.
activities.rationale: Higher-level metatext guides readers across the thesis (Bunton 1999; Hyland 2005); reading it alone tests whether it does that job.

activities.title: Metatext density check
learnerActions: Highlight all metatext in one chapter
Count instances per page and compare with a model thesis in your field
Remove redundant previews and repetitive formulae
Check every cross-reference against the current chapter numbering
activities.intendedInsight: Too little metatext leaves readers lost, while too much pads the text and can read as uncertain.
activities.rationale: Metadiscourse varies across fields and genres (Hyland 2005), so a local comparison is a better guide than a fixed rule.

difficulties.pattern: Every chapter begins 'In this chapter, I will…' followed by a list of section headings.
difficulties.revealedBy: Formulaic previews that duplicate the table of contents and do not state purpose or relation to the argument.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to state why the chapter is there before what it contains, and to vary language. Avoid forbidding previews, which are conventional and useful.

difficulties.pattern: Previews and cross-references refer to chapters that have since moved or been cut.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inaccurate 'see Chapter 4' references and previews that no longer match content.
difficulties.response: Recommend automatic cross-referencing in word processors and a final metatext check as a distinct editing pass.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to read aloud the first and last paragraphs of one chapter and say how they connect to the chapters before and after.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Paragraphs state the chapter's purpose and contribution and link explicitly to adjacent chapters and the research questions.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Paragraphs preview or summarise content but do not link to the wider argument.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No chapter introduction or conclusion, or paragraphs that are unrelated to the thesis argument.

guidance.contextNotes: PGT dissertations benefit from chapter introductions and conclusions but on a smaller scale. At PGR, metatext is essential to readability and is often added or revised in the final stages, and publication-based theses need linking text between papers.
reviewNotes: bunton1999metatext is a proposed reference; claims attributed to it are limited to its general subject (higher-level metatext in PhD theses).

guidance.summary: Proposals are persuasive, promissory genres read by evaluators under time pressure. Connor and Mauranen (1999) analysed EU research grant proposals and identified moves such as territory, gap, goal, means, reporting previous research, achievements, benefits, importance and competence claims, showing that proposals combine research-article moves with promotional ones. Creswell and Creswell (2018) give templates for qualitative, quantitative and mixed-methods proposals, and Paltridge and Starfield (2020) address doctoral proposals. Teach learners to analyse the specific template and criteria they face and to make alignment and feasibility visible.

activities.title: Criteria mapping
learnerActions: Obtain the assessment criteria for your proposal (admission, confirmation or funder)
Map each criterion to the section of your draft that addresses it
Identify criteria addressed weakly or not at all
Revise those sections and ask a peer to score the draft against the criteria
activities.intendedInsight: Proposals are evaluated against explicit criteria, and writers should address these visibly.
activities.rationale: Connor and Mauranen (1999) show that proposals include moves such as benefits and competence claims that respond to evaluators' needs rather than to purely academic conventions.

activities.title: Promissory language workshop
learnerActions: Collect future and conditional forms from funded proposals (will, aims to, is expected to, would enable)
Compare with language from completed-research articles
Revise your proposal to commit clearly to actions while hedging expected outcomes
activities.intendedInsight: Proposals commit firmly to what the researcher will do but calibrate claims about what will be found.
activities.rationale: Proposal templates (Creswell & Creswell 2018) separate planned procedures from anticipated outcomes, which calls for different degrees of commitment.

difficulties.pattern: My proposal explains the topic in depth but the methods are a paragraph and there is no timeline.
difficulties.revealedBy: Proposals that resemble essays, with extensive background and little design or feasibility detail.
difficulties.response: Use the criteria map to show reviewers' priorities, and ask for a Gantt-style timeline and a risk table.

difficulties.pattern: My study will prove that…
difficulties.revealedBy: Predetermined conclusions and boosted claims about outcomes of research not yet done.
difficulties.response: Distinguish what the researcher will do from what they expect to find, and practise hypothesis and expectation language.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to give a 90-second pitch of their proposal covering the problem, aims, approach, feasibility and significance.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Covers all elements concisely, with aims and approach clearly aligned and significance tailored to the audience.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Covers problem and aims well but is vague on approach or feasibility.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes the topic without stating aims, approach or significance.

guidance.contextNotes: On PG pre-sessionals, a short research proposal is a common extended-writing task and may contribute to progression decisions. PGT learners write dissertation proposals. PGR learners face admission proposals, confirmation or upgrade reports and, increasingly, fellowship and grant applications with funder-specific templates.

guidance.summary: Ethics documentation joins research integrity to plain-language writing. Creswell and Creswell (2018) set out ethical issues to anticipate at each stage of research, which can structure an application, and the Vitae RDF places ethics and research integrity within the professional conduct sub-domain (C1). For participant documents, the main EAP task is adapting register for a lay reader while preserving accuracy, which is mediation across audiences. Institutional templates take precedence and should be the starting point.

activities.title: Two-audience rewrite
learnerActions: Take a paragraph from your ethics application describing what participants will do
Rewrite it for a participant information sheet using plain language and direct address
Ask a peer outside your field to explain back what taking part involves
Revise any part they misunderstood
activities.intendedInsight: The same procedure must be described differently for a committee and for a participant, without loss of accuracy.
activities.rationale: Adapting register for a non-specialist audience is a mediation skill; comprehension checks with lay readers make clarity testable.

activities.title: Consistency audit
learnerActions: Place your methods description, ethics application and participant documents side by side
Check that sample, procedures, data storage and withdrawal arrangements match
Record and correct any discrepancies
activities.intendedInsight: Inconsistencies between documents can delay approval and raise integrity concerns later.
activities.rationale: Integrity requires that research is conducted as approved, which depends on consistent documentation (Vitae 2010, sub-domain C1).

difficulties.pattern: Participants will be informed that their data will be pseudonymised and stored in accordance with GDPR-compliant protocols.
difficulties.revealedBy: Participant sheets written in committee or legal register, with long sentences and technical terms.
difficulties.response: Model plain-language equivalents and use readability checks as a prompt for revision, not as a target. Keep required legal elements but explain them.

difficulties.pattern: Ethics is a bureaucratic hurdle, so I copy someone else's form and change the title.
difficulties.revealedBy: Applications that do not describe the actual study, and mismatched risks and procedures.
difficulties.response: Discuss the purpose of ethics review and the integrity implications of inaccurate applications.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain to you, as if you were a potential participant, what taking part in their study would involve and what happens to your data.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains clearly and accurately in plain language, including voluntariness, withdrawal and data handling.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Explains procedures but omits withdrawal or data use, or slips into technical language.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot give a clear account, or relies on jargon.

guidance.contextNotes: UG dissertations involving human participants usually require departmental ethics approval with simplified forms. PGT dissertations often involve first full applications. PGR applications may be complex, multi-site or international and may involve translated participant documents.
reviewNotes: No source in the current bibliography addresses the readability of participant information sheets directly; a reference from research-ethics or health-communication literature would strengthen this topic.

guidance.summary: Supervision is a relationship mediated by talk and text, and it is often where tacit disciplinary expectations become visible. Belcher (1994) studied three advisor–student pairs and linked the more successful relationship to a more reciprocal, collaborative stance and shared understanding of the target discourse community. Kamler and Thomson (2014) and Paltridge and Starfield (2020) treat supervision as a site of writing pedagogy, and Carless and Boud (2018) show that taking up feedback requires appreciating it, making judgements, managing affect and acting. Teach explicit expectation-setting and feedback negotiation, and treat indirectness in supervisor comments as a pragmatic issue.

activities.title: Expectation-setting conversation
learnerActions: Complete an expectations checklist covering meeting frequency, draft turnaround, feedback type and communication channels
Discuss it with your supervisor and agree a short written summary
Review the summary at an agreed point
activities.intendedInsight: Making expectations explicit reduces misunderstandings that might otherwise be attributed to language or personality.
activities.rationale: Belcher (1994) shows that mismatched understandings can undermine supervisory relationships; making them explicit is a practical response.

activities.title: Decoding feedback comments
learnerActions: Collect anonymised supervisor comments from your drafts
Classify each as directive, suggestion, question or praise, and rate how indirect it is
Write a response log stating what you changed for each comment or why you did not
Discuss any comments you were unsure about at the next meeting
activities.intendedInsight: Hedged comments are usually requests, and a response log makes engagement with feedback visible.
activities.rationale: Carless and Boud (2018) identify making judgements and taking action as components of feedback literacy; a response log operationalises both.

difficulties.pattern: My supervisor said 'you might want to think about' restructuring, so it's optional.
difficulties.revealedBy: Hedged suggestions left unaddressed and surprise when the supervisor repeats them more forcefully.
difficulties.response: Discuss how indirectness in English academic feedback often encodes requests, and practise clarifying ('Would you like me to restructure this before the next draft?'). Note that this varies by individual supervisor and that many first-language English students misread hedged advice too; clarity is a shared responsibility, so where possible encourage supervisors to mark which suggestions are requirements.

difficulties.pattern: The supervisor is the expert, so I must not disagree or ask for anything.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners who do not raise problems, accept all suggestions silently or wait months for feedback without asking.
difficulties.response: Explain institutional expectations of the supervisee's role, and practise mitigated requests and disagreements in role-play.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to draft the email they would send with their next chapter draft.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States the draft's stage, asks two or three specific questions, proposes a meeting and uses an appropriate register.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Sends the draft politely but with no specific questions or stage information.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sends the draft with no context or with an inappropriate register or demand.

guidance.contextNotes: UG dissertation supervision is usually brief and structured. PGT supervision is time-limited, so efficient agendas and specific requests matter. At PGR, supervision is a multi-year relationship, often with co-supervisors and formal progress reviews, and expectations differ by country and institution.
reviewNotes: Summary of Belcher (1994) is from memory of the study's design and main finding; check wording against the article.

guidance.summary: Kamler and Thomson (2014) reject the idea of 'writing up' at the end of research and treat writing as a way of doing research and of forming a scholarly identity, which supports writing from the start of a project. Self-regulation research (Zimmerman 2002) provides a cycle of forethought, performance and self-reflection that maps onto writing goals, monitoring and adjustment. Paltridge and Starfield (2020) discuss practical strategies for managing thesis writing. Writing groups and retreats are widely used in doctoral education; present them as options to try and evaluate, not as proven interventions.

activities.title: Writing log cycle
learnerActions: Set a weekly writing goal in terms of specific text
Log each session's time, output and obstacles
Review the log at the end of the week and adjust the next goal and strategy
Share one insight with a writing partner
activities.intendedInsight: Monitoring actual writing behaviour reveals patterns that intentions hide.
activities.rationale: The forethought–performance–reflection cycle of self-regulated learning (Zimmerman 2002) applied to writing.

activities.title: Writing group trial
learnerActions: Join or form a writing group that meets regularly for focused writing time
State a session goal at the start and report progress at the end
After four sessions, evaluate whether the group helps and adjust the format
activities.intendedInsight: Social structures can make writing regular and less isolating.
activities.rationale: Kamler and Thomson (2014) argue for social and pedagogical structures around doctoral writing; the specific format here is a proposal to test locally.

difficulties.pattern: I will start writing when I have finished reading and collecting data.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long periods with no written output and a last-minute writing crisis.
difficulties.response: Present writing as part of thinking and research (memos, draft sections, notes towards chapters). Avoid shaming; many writers have been taught that writing comes last.

difficulties.pattern: I keep rewriting the first chapter and never move on.
difficulties.revealedBy: Repeated versions of one section with little overall progress.
difficulties.response: Encourage separating generative drafting from revision, and set goals for new text. Refer to wellbeing services where anxiety is significant.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe a typical writing week and what they produced last week.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes a regular routine, text-specific goals and at least one support structure, and can name what was produced.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Writes regularly but with vague goals, or relies only on bursts before deadlines.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Has no routine or output and is postponing writing to a later stage.

guidance.contextNotes: PGT dissertation writing is compressed into a few months, so planning and routines matter most. PGR writing spans years, and sustained productivity, wellbeing and recovery from setbacks become central, often with institutional writing retreats and groups.

guidance.summary: Positionality writing draws on work on writer identity and self-mention. Ivanič (1998) distinguishes the autobiographical self, the discoursal self and the self as author, which helps writers separate useful reflexivity from personal narrative, and Tang and John (1999) and Hyland (2002) describe the roles authors take through first-person reference. Creswell and Creswell (2018) present reflexivity as a component of qualitative research reporting. Teach positionality statements as analytic, study-specific and linked to methodological decisions.

activities.title: From identity list to analytic statement
learnerActions: List aspects of your position relevant to the study (relationship to participants, language, professional role, theoretical commitments)
For each, write how it may have shaped access, data or interpretation
Note what you did about it
Draft a statement that keeps only the aspects that had consequences
activities.intendedInsight: Positionality is valuable when it explains effects and responses, not when it lists identity categories.
activities.rationale: Creswell and Creswell (2018) frame reflexivity in terms of how researcher background shapes interpretation, which this sequence makes explicit.

activities.title: First-person roles
learnerActions: Collect first-person uses from methodology and reflexivity sections in your field
Classify them by authorial role (representative, guide, recounter of procedures, opinion-holder, originator)
Check your own statement for the range of roles you use
activities.intendedInsight: First-person reference can perform different roles, and reflexive writing needs the more committed ones.
activities.rationale: Tang and John's (1999) typology of 'I' roles and Hyland's (2002) work on authorial identity support a role-based analysis.

difficulties.pattern: I was taught never to use 'I' in academic writing, so I write 'the researcher' throughout my positionality statement.
difficulties.revealedBy: Awkward third-person self-reference in sections where first person is conventional.
difficulties.response: Show field exemplars using 'I' in reflexive sections and discuss the myth of the absolute rule. Respect institutional or supervisory requirements where they genuinely differ.

difficulties.pattern: My positionality statement describes my life story and why I care about the topic.
difficulties.revealedBy: Biographical narratives with no link to methodological decisions or interpretation.
difficulties.response: Ask for each sentence 'So what for the study?' and cut or develop accordingly.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain how one aspect of their position might have affected one specific finding.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names a specific aspect, explains a plausible effect on a specific finding and describes what was done about it.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names a relevant aspect but the effect is general or no response is described.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Lists identity categories or describes personal motivation without consequences.

guidance.contextNotes: At PGT, positionality statements are mainly required in qualitative dissertations in education, health and social sciences. At PGR they are often integrated throughout the methodology and discussion and are probed in the viva. In many quantitative and experimental fields they are not expected.

guidance.summary: Hyland's (2004) analysis of dissertation acknowledgements identified a three-tier structure (reflecting, thanking and announcing moves) and showed the genre's role in self-presentation and academic networking. Article acknowledgements serve additional functions: disclosing funding and recognising contributors who do not meet authorship criteria (ICMJE, 2025; Brand et al., 2015). Teaching should combine move analysis with institutional and journal requirements and attention to confidentiality.

activities.title: Move analysis of acknowledgements
learnerActions: Analyse several thesis or dissertation acknowledgements from their field
Identify the moves and their order
Note variation in register and length
Draft their own acknowledgement
activities.intendedInsight: Acknowledgements follow recognisable conventions while allowing personal expression.
activities.rationale: Hyland (2004) identifies the moves of dissertation acknowledgements, providing a basis for analysis.

activities.title: Who goes where?
learnerActions: Sort a list of contributors into authors, acknowledged contributors and those not acknowledged
Justify decisions using ICMJE criteria or CRediT roles
Draft a funding statement
Compare decisions with peers
activities.intendedInsight: Acknowledgement and authorship are distinct, with ethical implications.
activities.rationale: Authorship criteria (ICMJE, 2025) and contributor role taxonomies (Brand et al., 2015) define who is acknowledged rather than listed as an author.

difficulties.pattern: Naming participants or organisations that were promised anonymity.
difficulties.revealedBy: Acknowledgements that identify research sites or participants by name.
difficulties.response: Check consent and ethics documentation before naming anyone; thank participants collectively where anonymity was promised.

difficulties.pattern: Register that is either extremely effusive or perfunctory.
difficulties.revealedBy: Very long, emotional acknowledgements or a single generic line.
difficulties.response: Show a range of models from the learner's field and institution and discuss audience.

difficulties.pattern: Offering authorship as a form of thanks, or acknowledging someone whose contribution merits authorship.
difficulties.revealedBy: Proposed author lists that include people who only provided resources, or acknowledgements of substantial intellectual contributors.
difficulties.response: Revisit authorship criteria and discuss with supervisors.

diagnostic.task: Give a list of contributors and ask the learner to decide who is acknowledged, who might be an author and how anonymous participants are thanked.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Correctly distinguishes authors and acknowledged contributors, includes funding details and protects anonymity.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mostly correct but omits funding or names an anonymous participant.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Confuses authorship and acknowledgement or omits required elements.

guidance.contextNotes: UG and PGT dissertation acknowledgements are usually short and optional. PGR thesis acknowledgements are longer and more personal. Article acknowledgements are formulaic and often include required funding and conflict-of-interest statements.
reviewNotes: Hyland (2004) is a proposed reference; verify before publication.

authorNotes: Overlap: res.literature-review and ges.literature-review-assignment. I have scoped the RES topic as positioning one's own study (judged by how it justifies questions and design) and made the GES topic a soft prerequisite. The GES authors should not make their topic depend on any RES topic, or a cycle will result.

Overlap: res.methods and dss.methodology-justification, and res.qualitative-reporting and dss.qualitative-writing. I deliberately did not link these in either direction to avoid cross-strand cycles; the editors should decide on the direction (I suggest the DSS topics depend on the RES ones, as their ESAP elaborations).

Cycle risk: RES/PUB topics depend softly on grp.dissertation-overview, grp.student-abstract, grp.project-proposal, ges.literature-review-assignment, dss.operationalising-concepts and exm.oral-exams. Those topics must not depend on any res.* or pub.* topic.

Gap: there is no topic for the doctoral confirmation or upgrade report (MPhil–PhD transfer, progression panels), a major UK PGR genre. I have folded it into res.research-proposal, but it differs, combining progress reporting, a draft chapter and a plan.

Gap: there is no topic on reporting guidelines and open-research statements (CONSORT, PRISMA, JARS, preregistration, data-availability and AI-use statements). These are partly covered in res.methods, res.quantitative-reporting and pub.cover-letters but deserve a topic.

Gap: there is no topic on turning a dissertation or thesis chapter into a journal article (reframing, cutting and re-positioning for a journal audience), a frequent PGR need distinct from both res.thesis-macrostructure and pub.journal-selection.

Gap: research article and thesis titles are covered only by ess.titles (essay titles). Research titles (colon titles, nominal versus verbal, disciplinary variation) may warrant a RES topic or a broadened ess.titles scope.
Mis-scoping: pub.academic-cv-bio bundles three dissimilar genres. Personal statements for postgraduate applications are mainly UG/PGT and might sit better in PRG or GRP, leaving CVs and bios in PUB.

Mis-scoping: grant and fellowship applications are bundled into res.research-proposal; they differ from doctoral proposals in audience, promotional moves (Connor & Mauranen 1999) and funder templates, and could be separated if the taxonomy grows.

Overlap: pub.research-engagement overlaps reg.non-specialist-audiences, grp.public-writing and grp.policy-brief. I made reg.non-specialist-audiences the hard prerequisite and left the GRP genres unlinked to avoid redundancy; the editors may prefer grp.public-writing as a soft prerequisite.
Placement: prg.acknowledgements covers thesis acknowledgements but sits in Academic Pragmatics; it could reasonably be cross-linked from res.thesis-macrostructure by its authors.
